experiences.title: Pentecost: wind, fire and tongues in Jerusalem
experiences.account: Acts 2:1-4 (KJV, public domain): "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Luke adds that pilgrims from many nations heard the disciples speaking in their own languages, that some mocked them as drunk, and that Peter explained the event as the fulfilment of Joel 2:28-32. About three thousand are said to have been baptised that day (Acts 2:41).
experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Luke presents the event as the promised outpouring of the Spirit (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8), the reversal of Babel and the birth of the Jerusalem church's mission. Peter's sermon reads it through Joel's prophecy of the 'last days'. Bystanders offered a naturalistic reading (drunkenness), which Peter rejects as it was only the third hour of the day.

assessments.text: Pentecost is the birthday of the Church and the inauguration of its sacramental life; the gift of the Spirit continues in baptism and chrismation/confirmation. Speaking in tongues is accepted as a real apostolic sign, though not regarded as the normative evidence of receiving the Spirit.

Acts 2 is a pattern, not only a one-off: a 'baptism in the Holy Spirit' distinct from conversion, often accompanied by tongues, is available to believers today. Classical Pentecostals (e.g. Assemblies of God) teach tongues as the 'initial physical evidence'.

Pentecost is a unique, unrepeatable redemptive-historical event marking the transition of the covenant; the tongues were real foreign languages that authenticated the apostolic message and ceased with the apostolic era.

Most critical scholars accept that the early Jesus movement experienced ecstatic phenomena (Paul's letters confirm glossolalia at Corinth), but see Luke's narrative, written perhaps 50 years later, as theologically shaped: the list of nations and the xenolalia motif serve his universal-mission theme.

debates: Were the 'tongues' known foreign languages (xenolalia), ecstatic speech (glossolalia), or a miracle of hearing?
Is Spirit baptism subsequent to conversion (Pentecostal) or identical with it (most Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox readings)?
Cessationism vs continuationism: is Acts 2 descriptive history or a normative pattern?

experiences.title: Paul's encounter on the Damascus road
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Acts 9:1-19 (also told in Acts 22 and 26): travelling to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus, Saul is surrounded by a light from heaven, falls to the ground and hears a voice asking why he persecutes him; the voice identifies itself as Jesus. Saul is left blind for three days until Ananias lays hands on him, 'something like scales' fall from his eyes and he is baptised. In his own letters Paul says only that God 'revealed his Son' in him (Galatians 1:15-16) and that the risen Christ 'appeared' to him last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8).

primarySource.title: Acts of the Apostles 9, 22, 26; Paul's letters

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: For Luke and Paul this was a resurrection appearance and a prophetic call to the Gentiles, not merely an inward change of mind. Paul treats it as the basis of his apostolic authority. In 2 Corinthians 12 he separately describes being 'caught up to the third heaven', which later mystics took as a model of rapture.

assessments.text: A genuine appearance of the risen Christ and the paradigm of conversion and vocation; the Feast of the Conversion of St Paul (25 January) has been kept in the West since the early Middle Ages.
A model for direct encounter with Christ, healing through the laying on of hands and being 'filled with the Holy Spirit' (Acts 9:17).

Paul's own testimony is first-hand and early (c. AD 50s), making this one of the best-attested religious experiences of antiquity; the three Acts versions differ in detail (who heard the voice, who saw the light), which scholars treat as Luke's literary variation.

Since William James the episode has been a classic case of sudden conversion; proposed explanations (guilt-driven crisis, temporal-lobe phenomena) are speculative and cannot be tested on a two-thousand-year-old report.

debates: Was Paul's experience 'objective' (seen by companions) or visionary? The Acts accounts differ.
Is Paul's conversion a 'conversion' at all, or a prophetic call within Judaism (Krister Stendahl's question)?

experiences.title: The Spirit falls on Cornelius' household at Caesarea
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Acts 10-11: the Roman centurion Cornelius sees an angel in a vision telling him to send for Peter; at Joppa Peter has a trance-vision of a sheet of clean and unclean animals and hears 'what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common'. While Peter is preaching in Cornelius' house the Holy Spirit 'fell on all them which heard the word' and they speak with tongues; Peter then has them baptised. In Acts 19:1-7 a similar sequence occurs at Ephesus, where Paul lays hands on about twelve disciples who speak with tongues and prophesy.
experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: In Acts the event settles a controversy: the visible gift of the Spirit to uncircumcised Gentiles convinces the Jerusalem church that Gentiles may be baptised without first becoming Jews, and is cited again at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:8).

assessments.text: One of the key 'Pentecostal' texts: tongues accompany the coming of the Spirit here as at Pentecost and Ephesus, supporting the doctrine of tongues as initial evidence.
Tongues served here as a one-time public sign that Gentiles were included in the people of God; the episode is descriptive and transitional, not a template for later believers.
The sequence of Spirit, baptism and (at Ephesus) laying on of hands is read in light of baptism and confirmation; the visions show God guiding the Church's apostolic leaders.
Luke uses the episode to legitimate the Gentile mission, a real and divisive issue in the 40s-50s also visible in Galatians 2; the details are shaped by his narrative purpose.

debates: Does the order of events (Spirit before baptism) undermine any fixed sacramental sequence?
Are the Acts tongues-episodes normative or transitional?

experiences.title: The New Prophecy of Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla

place.name: Pepuza, Phrygia (near modern Karayakuplu, Uşak, Turkey)

experiences.account: Paraphrase of the hostile sources preserved by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 5.16-18) and Epiphanius (Panarion 48): in Phrygia a recent convert, Montanus, fell into a frenzied, ecstatic state and began to prophesy in an unusual manner, speaking in the first person as the voice of God; two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, did the same. The oracles called for stricter fasting, readiness for martyrdom and a coming descent of the New Jerusalem at Pepuza. Maximilla is reported to have said that after her there would be no more prophet, but the end.

primarySource.title: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.16-19 (quoting an anonymous anti-Montanist writer and Apollonius)
primarySource.citation: Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 5.16.7-9; Epiphanius, Panarion 48.4; Tertullian, De anima 9

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Asian bishops held synods against the movement and some tried to exorcise the prophetesses. Critics objected less to prophecy itself than to its ecstatic, 'unnatural' form, its claim to supersede apostolic teaching and its failed predictions. In Carthage Tertullian embraced the New Prophecy (c. 207) as the Paraclete's discipline for a mature church.

assessments.text: The early church judged Montanism a false prophecy, a key reason prophecy was tested by conformity to apostolic tradition and the bishops' teaching; the episode helped define the closing of public revelation.

Many Pentecostal historians see the Montanists as partly a charismatic movement suppressed by an institutionalising church, while acknowledging the excesses; others hold them up as a warning against prophecy that claims new doctrine.
Montanism is an early illustration of why continuing revelatory prophecy threatens the sufficiency of Scripture.

Inscriptions and the identification of Pepuza (2000s) show a long-lived Phrygian church with women clergy; nearly all our textual evidence comes from opponents, so the movement's self-understanding is hard to recover.

debates: Ecstatic vs. rational prophecy: early critics argued true prophets did not lose self-control.
Can later prophecy add to apostolic revelation?
Women's leadership: Montanist prophetesses were a key point of attack.

experiences.title: Perpetua's prison visions at Carthage
experiences.account: Paraphrase of the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, chs. 3-10, which presents itself as Perpetua's own prison diary: asked by her brother to request a vision, she sees a bronze ladder to heaven guarded by a dragon, climbs it and is welcomed by a shepherd in a garden who gives her cheese-like curd; she later sees her dead brother Dinocrates suffering and, after her prayers, refreshed; on the eve of the games she dreams she is made a man and defeats an Egyptian gladiator, and understands she will fight the devil and win. She and her slave Felicity were executed in the arena on 7 March 203.

primarySource.title: The Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The editor, possibly sympathetic to the New Prophecy, presents the visions as proof that the Spirit still gives 'new visions' in the last days (Joel 2). Augustine later preached on her feast and felt bound to argue that the Dinocrates vision did not imply salvation for the unbaptised.

assessments.text: Perpetua and Felicity are commemorated in the Roman canon of the Mass; the visions are revered as a martyr's graces, while the Dinocrates vision is cited in debates on prayer for the dead.
Valued as an authentic early witness to costly faith; the prayer-for-the-dead element is usually treated as a historical curiosity rather than doctrine.
Widely accepted as one of the earliest surviving texts by a Christian woman. Scholars debate how much the Montanist-leaning editor shaped it and how to read its dream imagery.
The dreams have been read as a young mother's processing of family conflict, gender and impending death (e.g. the gender reversal in the final vision).

debates: Montanist influence on the text.
Prayer for the dead and the Dinocrates vision.

experiences.title: Antony and the Desert Fathers: combat with demons and the flame of prayer

place.name: Inner Mountain (Monastery of St Antony, Eastern Desert of Egypt)

experiences.account: Paraphrase of Athanasius' Life of Antony and the Sayings of the Desert Fathers: after withdrawing into the desert (c. 285), Antony is assailed by demons in the form of beasts and soldiers, and after a long struggle sees the roof open and a beam of light descend, and the pain cease. Emerging after twenty years, he is described as neither emaciated nor overfed, heals the sick and casts out demons. In the Sayings, Abba Joseph answers a monk asking what more he can do by stretching his hands to heaven, his fingers becoming like ten lamps of fire, and saying that he may become all flame.

primarySource.title: Athanasius, Life of Antony
primarySource.citation: Athanasius, Vita Antonii 8-10; 14; Apophthegmata Patrum (alphabetical), Joseph of Panephysis 7

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: For Athanasius, Antony embodies Christ's victory over demons and a life lived in the strength of the incarnate Word; the Life quickly became a bestseller and helped spread monasticism (it features in Augustine's conversion story). The desert tradition was also cautious: many sayings warn monks against seeking visions and against demons appearing as angels of light.

assessments.text: The desert fathers are the root of Orthodox spirituality; their discernment (diakrisis) and stress on humility over visions shape Orthodox caution toward extraordinary experiences.
Antony is the father of monasticism; the Life is read as a classic of spiritual combat, though modern Catholic scholarship recognises its hagiographical style.
The Reformers admired the desert fathers' devotion but rejected monastic vows as a superior way; miracle stories are generally treated as legendary embellishment.
Antony is historical (letters attributed to him survive), but the Life is shaped by Athanasius' anti-Arian and ecclesiastical aims (David Brakke); demon narratives reflect late antique cosmology.

debates: Discernment of spirits: the desert tradition's warnings about deceptive visions.
Historicity of hagiography.

experiences.title: Augustine's conversion in the Milan garden: 'Take up and read'
experiences.account: Confessions 8.12 (trans. E.B. Pusey, 1838, public domain): weeping under a fig tree, Augustine hears from a neighbouring house a child's voice chanting 'Take up and read; take up and read.' He opens the apostle's letters at Romans 13:13-14 and reports that 'by a light as it were of serenity infused into my heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished away.' He was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. Months later at Ostia he and his mother Monica shared a brief contemplative ascent (Confessions 9.10).
experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Augustine himself interprets the voice as a divine command, comparing it to Antony's hearing of the Gospel in church. The Confessions frame the moment as the climax of grace overcoming a divided will.

assessments.text: A classic of grace-wrought conversion valued by both Catholic and Protestant traditions; Luther and Calvin read it as a witness to the priority of grace.
Augustine is honoured as a saint in Orthodoxy but his theology is received with reservations; the conversion story is admired as a personal testimony.

Written about eleven years later (c. 397-400), the account is a carefully crafted literary-theological narrative; scholars (e.g. Pierre Courcelle) debated how literally to take the child's voice, though most accept a real crisis in the garden.
William James used Augustine as a classic case of the 'divided self' resolved in conversion.

debates: How much of the Confessions is literary construction?
Grace and free will: Augustine's conversion as a template for his later anti-Pelagian theology.

experiences.title: Symeon the New Theologian's visions of divine light
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Symeon's Catechetical Discourses (esp. 22), where he describes himself in the third person as a young man named George: praying at night, he is suddenly flooded with a divine light that fills the room; he loses awareness of the walls and of himself, and is filled with tears and joy. In his Hymns of Divine Love he speaks repeatedly of seeing Christ as light and insists that those who say no one can now experience God consciously deny the gospel.

primarySource.title: Symeon the New Theologian, Catechetical Discourses and Hymns of Divine Love
primarySource.citation: Catechesis 22; Hymns of Divine Love (e.g. Hymn 25)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Symeon's claims and his veneration of his own spiritual father caused conflict with church authorities; he was exiled from Constantinople c. 1009 but later rehabilitated. Orthodoxy came to call him 'New Theologian', one of only three so titled (with John the Evangelist and Gregory of Nazianzus).

assessments.text: A canonical teacher of the conscious experience of grace; his insistence that the Spirit's indwelling is felt, not just believed, anticipates hesychasm.
Respected as an Eastern mystic; Catholic theology generally distinguishes such experience from the created grace it posits, a difference sharpened later in the Palamite debate.

Some charismatic writers point to Symeon's 'baptism in the Spirit' language (tears, experiential certainty) as an Eastern parallel to Spirit baptism, while Orthodox scholars caution against equating the two.
His conflict with Stephen of Nicomedia illustrates the perennial tension between charismatic authority and ecclesiastical office in Byzantium.

debates: Charism vs. office: can an unordained or junior monk bind or loose by spiritual authority?
Is conscious experience of grace normal for all Christians?

experiences.title: Hesychasm and the uncreated light of Tabor
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Gregory Palamas' Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts (1338-41): monks practising stillness (hesychia), with the Jesus Prayer and controlled breathing, report seeing an ineffable light. Palamas argues this is not a created or symbolic light but the same uncreated divine light that shone from Christ at the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor (Matthew 17:2): the energies of God, in which humans truly participate, while God's essence remains unknowable.

primarySource.title: Gregory Palamas, Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The Calabrian monk Barlaam mocked the hesychasts as 'navel-gazers' (omphalopsychoi) and argued any light seen must be created. Councils at Constantinople (1341, 1347, 1351) upheld Palamas; he became Archbishop of Thessalonica and was canonised in 1368.

assessments.text: The essence-energies distinction is dogmatic for most Orthodox theologians: deification (theosis) is real participation in God's uncreated energies, and the light of Tabor is its foretaste. The second Sunday of Lent honours Palamas.

Historically many Western theologians judged the essence-energies distinction a compromise of divine simplicity; since the 20th century many Catholic scholars see it as compatible with, or complementary to, Thomist teaching.
Generally unfamiliar until recently; some Reformed critics share the divine-simplicity objection, while others see parallels with union-with-Christ theology.

The breathing technique and light visions have been compared with Sufi dhikr and other contemplative methods; the controversy was also bound up with Byzantine civil war politics (Kantakouzenos vs. the regency).

debates: Essence vs. energies and divine simplicity.
Is the light created or uncreated?
Psychosomatic prayer methods: legitimate aid or mechanical technique?

experiences.title: Hildegard of Bingen's 'living light'
experiences.account: Paraphrase of the Protestificatio (preface) of Scivias: in 1141, when she was forty-two years and seven months old, a fiery light of great brilliance came from the open heavens and poured into her whole brain and heart, and she suddenly understood the meaning of the Psalter, the Gospels and the other Scriptures. She insists she saw these things not in dreams, sleep or frenzy but awake, with the eyes and ears of the inner self. Later she described a lesser 'shadow of the living light' that was always with her.

primarySource.title: Hildegard of Bingen, Scivias (Know the Ways), 1141-51
primarySource.citation: Scivias, Protestificatio; Letter to Guibert of Gembloux (1175)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Hildegard wrote to Bernard of Clairvaux for reassurance, and Pope Eugenius III had parts of Scivias read at the Synod of Trier (1147-48) and encouraged her to continue writing, giving her unusual authority to preach and correspond with emperors and popes as a prophetess.

assessments.text: Canonised (equivalent canonisation) and declared a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XVI in 2012; her visions are regarded as authentic private revelation integrated into sound theology.
Often valued as a creative theologian, composer and naturalist, and as an example of a woman's prophetic voice, without accepting all her visionary claims as revelation.

Charles Singer (1917) and Oliver Sacks suggested her descriptions of light and fortification-like patterns resemble migraine aura; this does not settle the religious question of meaning, as Sacks himself noted.
Her visionary authority let a woman speak publicly in a church that barred women from preaching; scholars such as Barbara Newman stress how she navigated this 'prophetic' role.

debates: Migraine hypothesis and naturalistic explanation.
Women's authority through visionary prophecy.

experiences.title: Francis of Assisi receives the stigmata at La Verna
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Thomas of Celano (First Life, 1229) and Bonaventure (Major Legend 13): around the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) 1224, while fasting on Mount La Verna, Francis sees a seraph with six wings, fixed to a cross. As the vision fades, marks like nails appear in his hands and feet and a wound in his side. Brother Elias' letter announcing Francis' death (1226) is the earliest text to mention the marks.

primarySource.title: Thomas of Celano, First Life of St Francis; Bonaventure, Legenda Maior
primarySource.citation: Celano, Vita prima 94-95; Bonaventure, Legenda Maior 13.3; Letter of Elias of Cortona (1226); Francis' autograph 'Chartula' blessing for Brother Leo

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Contemporaries took the stigmata as a seal showing Francis as an 'alter Christus'. Some Dominicans and secular clergy questioned the claim; Pope Gregory IX issued bulls (1237) defending it. It is generally considered the first reported case of stigmata.

assessments.text: The stigmata are commemorated in a feast (17 September) and widely accepted as a supernatural grace, though the Church does not require belief in them.
Orthodox tradition has no stigmatics and is reserved about the phenomenon, seeing a Western emphasis on imitating Christ's physical suffering that differs from Eastern stress on transfiguration.
Usually doubtful or agnostic; Francis is widely admired for poverty and peacemaking, but the stigmata are often attributed to pious embellishment.

Elias' early letter and multiple witnesses make the claim of visible marks well attested as a belief; explanations range from genuine wounds of unknown cause to self-inflicted or psychosomatic wounds or later elaboration (André Vauchez discusses the sources).

debates: Authenticity and possible natural causes of stigmata.
Why stigmata appear almost exclusively in Latin Catholicism after 1224.

experiences.title: Catherine of Siena: mystical espousal and invisible stigmata
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Raymond of Capua's Legenda Maior: Catherine experienced a 'mystical marriage' to Christ (c. 1368) and, at Pisa on 1 April 1375, after communion, rays from the crucified Christ pierced her hands, feet and side; at her prayer the wounds remained invisible, causing pain but no marks. Her disciples recorded her dictating The Dialogue while in ecstasy (1377-78).

primarySource.title: Raymond of Capua, Life of Catherine of Siena; Catherine, The Dialogue
primarySource.citation: Raymond of Capua, Legenda Maior 2.6 (stigmata); The Dialogue (1378)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Her ecstatic authority lent weight to her letters urging Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome (1376-77). Franciscans contested Dominican claims of her stigmata; Pope Sixtus IV (a Franciscan) at one point forbade depicting them.

assessments.text: Saint, Doctor of the Church (1970) and co-patron of Europe; her mystical experiences are treated as authentic graces, though the invisible-stigmata claim is not a matter of faith.
Admired for courageous church reform and social service; extreme fasting and ecstatic claims are often viewed critically.
Caroline Walker Bynum interprets her extreme fasting and eucharistic piety as a form of female religious agency; Raymond's Life is hagiography written to support canonisation.
Her refusal of food has been debated as 'holy anorexia' (Rudolph Bell), a diagnosis others reject as anachronistic.

debates: Female mystics, fasting and authority.
Rivalry between religious orders over stigmata claims.

experiences.title: Julian of Norwich's sixteen 'showings'
experiences.account: Paraphrase with short quotation from Revelations of Divine Love (Long Text): at thirty and a half years old, on 8 or 13 May 1373, gravely ill and given the last rites, Julian gazes at a crucifix and receives sixteen 'showings' over a night and day: the bleeding head of Christ, a hazelnut-sized thing representing 'all that is made', and Christ telling her that sin is 'behovely' and that 'all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' (ch. 27). She recovers, and spends some twenty years reflecting on their meaning, including Christ as Mother.

primarySource.title: Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love (Short and Long Texts)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Julian lived as an anchoress at St Julian's church, Norwich. Margery Kempe records consulting her about discernment of her own visions (c. 1413), and Julian advised testing whether they led to charity and conformity with the faith.

assessments.text: Venerated (her feast is kept locally) and widely read; her optimism about divine love is admired, while some theologians ask how her near-universal hope fits Church teaching on judgement.
Commemorated on 8 May in the Church of England; often treated as a mother of English spiritual writing.
Appreciated for devotion to the cross; some critics question the 'Christ as Mother' imagery and hints of universalism.
Her texts are well documented (manuscripts c. 15th-17th c.); the Short Text may date from the 1380s, the Long from the 1390s-1410s. Her illness-and-recovery narrative is plausibly autobiographical.

debates: Universal salvation hints ('all shall be well').
Feminine imagery for God.
Discernment criteria for private revelation.

experiences.title: Teresa of Ávila: the transverberation and interior castle
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Teresa's Life (Libro de la vida, ch. 29): she sees beside her a small, very beautiful angel holding a long golden spear with a point of fire, which he seems to thrust several times into her heart; drawing it out, he leaves her wholly on fire with love of God, the pain so great it makes her moan yet the sweetness so excessive she does not wish it to stop. She describes the pain as spiritual, though the body shares in it. She also reports raptures and levitations which embarrassed her, and later maps prayer as seven 'mansions' in The Interior Castle (1577).

primarySource.title: Teresa of Ávila, The Book of Her Life; The Interior Castle
primarySource.citation: Libro de la vida 29.13; 20 (raptures); Moradas del castillo interior (1577)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Teresa wrote under obedience to confessors, amid the Spanish Inquisition's suspicion of alumbrados (illuminists) and women visionaries; the Inquisition examined the Life. Several confessors initially told her the visions were demonic. Her reform founded the Discalced Carmelites with John of the Cross.

assessments.text: Canonised 1622 and the first woman Doctor of the Church (1970); her teaching on prayer is a benchmark of orthodox mysticism. The transverberation is commemorated by the Carmelites (26 August) and Bernini's sculpture in Rome.
Her writings are widely read for prayer; many Protestants question raptures and levitations while valuing her realism, humour and Christ-centredness.
Some charismatics draw parallels between her raptures and Spirit-filled experiences; she herself warned that such favours are not the measure of holiness.

Read in the context of the Inquisition, gender and converso ancestry (her grandfather was a Jewish convert); 20th-century psychiatry speculated about hysteria or epilepsy, interpretations now regarded as reductive.

debates: Discernment under the Inquisition: illuminism vs. orthodox mysticism.
Bodily phenomena (levitation) and their value.

experiences.title: John of the Cross: the Toledo prison and the 'dark night'
experiences.account: Paraphrase from early biographies and John's own works: seized in December 1577 by Calced Carmelites opposed to Teresa's reform, John is held for about nine months in a tiny cell in Toledo, flogged and underfed. There he composes much of the Spiritual Canticle. He escapes in August 1578. In The Dark Night and The Ascent of Mount Carmel he teaches that the soul is purified by passing through 'nights' of sense and spirit, and warns against attaching importance to visions, locutions and other extraordinary phenomena: the soul should rest in faith alone.

primarySource.title: John of the Cross, The Dark Night; Ascent of Mount Carmel; Spiritual Canticle
primarySource.citation: Ascent of Mount Carmel 2.11 (on rejecting visions); Dark Night 1-2

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: John's teaching was in part a corrective: mystical union is a work of love and faith, not of sensational experiences; this caution became standard Catholic discernment teaching.

assessments.text: Canonised 1726 and Doctor of the Church (1926); 'dark night' theology underpins Catholic spiritual direction.
Orthodox writers find parallels with apophatic theology and the desert fathers' warnings about visions, while noting differences of emphasis.
Read by many evangelicals and Anglicans as a guide to spiritual dryness; some critics fear an overly ascetic, passive spirituality.
'Dark night of the soul' has been compared with depression; spiritual directors and psychologists (e.g. Gerald May) distinguish the two by fruits such as deepened love and freedom.

debates: Visions vs. naked faith: John's critique of extraordinary phenomena.
Spiritual desolation and depression.

experiences.title: Ignatius of Loyola at Manresa and the Spiritual Exercises
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Ignatius' Autobiography (dictated 1553-55, in the third person as 'the pilgrim'): convalescing from a cannonball wound (1521), he reads lives of Christ and the saints and notices the different 'spirits' that leave him consoled or desolate. At Manresa (1522-23) he passes through scruples nearly to despair, then receives illuminations: seeing the Trinity as three keys of a musical instrument, the creation of the world, and, sitting by the river Cardoner, an understanding so great that everything seemed new to him. From these experiences he drafts the Spiritual Exercises, including rules for the discernment of spirits.

primarySource.title: Ignatius of Loyola, Autobiography (Reminiscences); Spiritual Exercises

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The Inquisition questioned Ignatius in Alcalá and Salamanca on suspicion of being an alumbrado; he was cleared. The Exercises were approved by Pope Paul III in 1548 and became the foundation of Jesuit formation.

assessments.text: The Exercises are among the most influential retreat methods in Catholicism; Ignatian discernment (consolation and desolation) is widely used.
Historically suspicious of the Jesuits, many Protestants now use adapted Ignatian prayer and imaginative reading of the Gospels.

The Autobiography is late and shaped for Jesuit edification, but Ignatius' visionary period and his examination by the Inquisition are documented; John O'Malley stresses the Exercises' practical, pastoral character.
The attention to inner movements has been compared with modern psychology of emotion; T.M. Luhrmann studied related imaginative prayer practices among evangelicals.

debates: Discernment of spirits as a method.
Imagination in prayer: aid or danger?
